variants.name: AbortController / AbortSignal loop with awaited completion
variants.implementation_notes: On the event loop the latch is an AbortSignal: abort() is phase 1 (one-way, sets reason, notifies 'abort' listeners and rejects signal-aware APIs) and awaiting the worker's promise is phase 2, because the loop's finally block is where flush and release run. AbortSignal replaces the classic shared boolean and is already threaded through fetch, streams, timers and most libraries. The classic flag form still appears in legacy code, but a bare boolean plus setInterval polling is strictly worse than the signal.
pitfalls: An AbortSignal is single-use and one-way: after abort it cannot be reset, so a restarted worker needs a fresh controller, not a reused signal (any API called with the aborted signal rejects immediately).
Node does not wait for pending promises at process exit: an unawaited shutdown promise loses buffered writes - keep the loop alive until the cleanup promise settles.
Abort listeners must be removed or added with { once: true }; a long-lived signal otherwise retains their closures and everything they reference, as MDN documents.
Cancellation only reaches APIs that take the signal: a tight synchronous loop or a blocking call ignores abort() completely and must be rewritten around await points.

variants.name: node:worker_threads shutdown message + 'exit'
variants.implementation_notes: For a real thread the two phases are a message and an event: postMessage is phase 1, the worker finishes its current item, flushes and exits (phase 2 inside the worker), and once(worker, 'exit') is the caller's completion step. worker.terminate() is the forced fallback - it stops JavaScript execution as soon as possible and returns when 'exit' fires, so it must not be the normal path. This variant is the right binding when the participant is CPU-bound or owns native/stdio resources in another thread.
pitfalls: worker.terminate() stops all JavaScript execution in the thread as soon as possible and skips in-worker cleanup: it is the fallback, and in-flight writes or half-released handles are the price.

An 'exit' listener alone does not prove cleanup ran - the worker can exit on an uncaught exception or an explicit process.exit before its flush resolved; have it acknowledge completion (or make the flush synchronous/awaited before exit).
Messages are asynchronous: the worker may be mid-item when the shutdown message arrives, so the handler must finish or abandon that item explicitly rather than dropping it.
